title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship to review, fix and approve code. Nvidia brings back Jensen Huang and its shares jump 31.5%, ChatGPT’s Chat tab moves to GPT-6.2, and Claude puts connectors and skills together as plugins. An Anthropic study finds AI slowing hiring rather than causing layoffs, two US states sue SpaceX over Grok deepfakes, and Z.ai releases GLM-5.4.
summary: Claude Ship, in beta for Team and Enterprise on GitHub, reviews pull requests, fixes failing checks and approves routine changes a team’s policy allows. Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after pressure from President Trump; its shares closed up 31.5%. ChatGPT’s Chat tab is moving to a version of GPT-6.2 Sol for paid users, and GPT-5.6 retires on 23 December. Claude’s connectors and skills now live together as plugins, with Team plans getting the change from 30 November. Anthropic’s interviews with 58 customers found few AI layoffs but two-thirds hiring less. Virginia and Oregon sued SpaceX over sexual deepfakes made with Grok, and Z.ai released GLM-5.4, a ‘loop transformer’ model, in its coding plan.
uncertainty: Claude Ship’s approval agent and PR Steward are in beta, and Anthropic’s figures on its own team are self-reported. Nvidia’s share price will move; its investigations and the 3 December Senate hearing are still ahead. GPT-6.2 scores are OpenAI’s own internal tests. The Anthropic study is interviews with its own customers, not a random sample. The state lawsuits are allegations that courts have not yet tested. Z.ai has published no coding benchmarks for GLM-5.4 itself, and its open weights have no date.

stories.theme: Anthropic’s Claude Ship reviews pull requests, fixes them and approves the routine ones a team’s written policy allows
stories.changed: On 23 November 2026 Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta for Claude Team and Enterprise customers whose code is on GitHub. It has three parts. Code Review, already generally available, checks pull requests and posts findings. PR Steward, new and in beta, works on failing automated checks, merge conflicts and review comments, and after every push says what it changed and how to undo it; it is designed not to approve or merge. Claude Approvals, also in beta, reads an approval policy the team writes as a file in the repository, approves routine changes the policy allows and sends the rest to the people it names. Anthropic recommends starting it in observe mode, where it posts its decision but approves nothing. Developers can also type /ship in Claude Code to push a change, open the pull request and have Claude work on feedback and failing checks. It is billed on tokens, with spend limits for Code Review and PR Steward, and is not available to organisations using zero data retention, the HIPAA setup or customer-managed encryption keys. Anthropic says that on its Claude Code team, merged pull requests more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%.
stories.matters: Code is now written faster than people can review it. Claude Ship moves review, fixes and some approvals to AI under rules a team writes down, so the real question becomes which changes still need a person.
stories.imply: Letting an AI approve code is a policy decision, not just a setting. Costs grow with the number and size of pull requests, and a policy that uses Claude’s review triggers billed reviews even in observe mode.
uses: Write down which folders or kinds of change always need a human, such as payments, security or database migrations, before switching approvals on.
Run Claude Approvals in observe mode for a few weeks and compare its decisions with your reviewers’.
Set a monthly spend limit per repository and check the bill after the first busy week.
stories.example: A platform team lets Claude approve documentation and test-only changes, requires two engineers on anything touching the billing service, and keeps the policy file in the repository so changes to the rules are reviewed too.
stories.audience: Engineering managers, developers on Claude Team or Enterprise plans, and security and compliance leads who sign off on code changes.
stories.watch: How many teams move from observe mode to letting Claude approve, how mistakes are caught, and whether GitHub and OpenAI answer with similar approval agents.

source.title: Anthropic: Introducing Claude Ship, 23 November 2026
source.quote: Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios.

stories.theme: Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang as chief executive after pressure from President Trump, and its shares jumped 31.5% in a day
stories.changed: Nvidia said on Monday 23 November 2026 that its board had unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, 11 days after he resigned over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman accused of ties to Beijing; its filing dates the board’s decision to 22 November. Reuters says the reversal came under pressure from President Trump, who told CNBC his intervention was “very important”. The board said US government input left it confident that his return “poses no national security risk”. Nvidia shares closed up 31.5%, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, though not enough to erase all losses since he left on 12 November. CNBC says the Nasdaq rose 6.51%, its best day since April 2025, with Dell up 20.46% and CoreWeave up 22.32%. Lawmakers from both parties objected. The board has set up committees on possible foreign intelligence targeting of Huang and on export controls, and Huang will testify at a public Senate hearing on 3 December. Reuters also reports that some customers in China had cancelled or delayed orders while he was away.
stories.matters: Nvidia makes most of the chips behind AI services, and its share price has become a gauge for the whole AI trade. One day’s rally changes no products, but it eases pressure on AI firms that depend on investors.
stories.imply: The hard questions remain: accounting and export-control probes, a shareholder lawsuit and doubts about the board’s independence. Expect more swings, especially around the Senate hearing.
uses: Do not read one day’s rally as the end of AI budget pressure; keep the supplier checks you started last week.
If you rent GPU cloud capacity, ask your provider how export rules and chip supply could affect your contract.
Note the 3 December hearing if your firm relies on Nvidia hardware or GPU cloud providers.
stories.example: A finance lead updating next year’s AI budget keeps two price scenarios for GPU cloud time instead of assuming either last week’s fall or this week’s rebound will last.
stories.audience: Finance teams, IT buyers of cloud and GPU capacity, and anyone following AI company valuations.
stories.watch: The Senate Banking Committee hearing on 3 December, the board’s investigations, and whether customers in China come back.

source.title: Reuters: Huang returns as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervention in abrupt board reversal, 23 November 2026
source.quote: The stock closed up 31.5%, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, vaulting the chipmaker back to the position of the second-biggest company by market value after Apple

stories.theme: ChatGPT’s everyday Chat tab moves to GPT-6.2 for paid users, and older GPT-5.6 models retire on 23 December
stories.changed: On 23 November 2026 OpenAI began rolling out a version of GPT-6.2 Sol tuned for everyday conversation to the Chat tab for Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users worldwide, replacing GPT-6 there; Enterprise availability depends on admin settings. The models in ChatGPT Work and Codex do not change. In OpenAI’s own tests it scored 71.7% on image understanding against 47.4% for GPT-6, followed instructions on especially hard prompts 78.1% of the time against 62.5%, and at the lowest reasoning setting scored 65% on expert-level tasks against 52%. On an internal version of the BrowseComp web-search test it scored 64.5% against 54.4% at the Extra high setting. OpenAI says it is also better at offering useful follow-ups, such as telling you when a price drops. Separately, ChatGPT said GPT-5.6 Sol will be retired from Chat, Work and Codex, and GPT-5.6 Terra from Work and Codex, on 23 December.
stories.matters: This is the model most paid ChatGPT users will now meet by default. Better image reading and instruction following help with ordinary work: screenshots, forms, charts and long briefs.
stories.imply: Answers to the same prompt may change. Saved prompts or team workflows that rely on GPT-5.6 have a month before that model goes.
uses: Re-run two or three prompts your team relies on and check the output still fits.
Try it on a photo of a form, chart or sign, and check what it read against the original.
If anyone uses GPT-5.6 in Work or Codex, move and test their work before 23 December.
stories.example: A support lead pastes a customer’s screenshot of an error message and asks ChatGPT to draft a reply, then checks the error code it read against the image before sending.
stories.audience: Paid ChatGPT users, workspace admins and teams with saved prompts or custom GPTs.
stories.watch: Whether free users get it, and how OpenAI handles the GPT-5.6 switch-off for teams that chose that model.

source.title: OpenAI Help Center: ChatGPT release notes, 23 November 2026
source.quote: In our tests in the Chat tab, it scored 71.7% on image understanding, up from 47.4% for GPT‑6.

stories.theme: Claude puts connectors and skills together as plugins, and Team admins should check one setting before 30 November
stories.changed: On 23 November 2026 Anthropic brought connectors (links to tools such as email, drives or a CRM) and skills (saved instructions that teach Claude a task) together as plugins. In Claude, Customize in the sidebar becomes Plugins, and one Plugins page replaces the separate Skills, Connectors and Plugins tabs, with filters for skills or connectors and labels marking public plugins as Verified or Community. Claude says more than 10,000 plugins are available to browse. The change is live on Free, Pro, Max and Ultra plans; Team plans get it gradually from 30 November and Enterprise plans in the following weeks. Existing connectors, skills and plugins stay installed, but removing a plugin that bundles a connector does not disconnect that connector. From 30 November, Team and Enterprise organisations that have Skills switched off will also have plugins blocked in the Claude Desktop app.
stories.matters: One place to find and switch on add-ons makes it easier to plug Claude into the tools you work in, and also easier to install something written by a stranger.
stories.imply: Admins have a decision to make before 30 November, and users should check what a Community plugin can reach before installing it. Under the HIPAA setup, plugins, skills and connectors are not covered by the agreement.
uses: Open Plugins, filter to connectors and remove the ones you no longer use; disconnect them separately.
Prefer Verified plugins for work data, and read what a Community plugin connects to first.
Admins: decide before 30 November whether to turn Skills on so plugins keep working in Claude Desktop.
stories.example: An IT admin at a 40-person firm turns Skills on before 30 November, then shares a short list of approved plugins for the team’s CRM and shared drive.
stories.audience: Claude users, Team and Enterprise admins, and security teams that vet add-ons.
stories.watch: The Team rollout from 30 November, and how Anthropic reviews Community plugins.

source.title: Claude Help Center: Manage plugins, skills, and connectors from one Plugins page, November 2026
source.quote: Removing a plugin that packages skills and a connector doesn't disconnect its connector, so you'll need to disconnect it separately.

stories.theme: Anthropic interviewed 58 business customers: few AI layoffs, but two-thirds say AI means they are hiring less
stories.changed: On 23 November 2026 Anthropic economists published “Working with AI”, based on 66 interviews with people at 58 of its enterprise customers. They found very few layoffs driven by AI: people at only two companies had seen AI automation fully eliminate a job, and five described pushing out staff who would not adopt AI. But people at two-thirds of the companies said they were hiring less because of AI, mostly by not adding staff they would otherwise have needed to grow, while 10 companies were hiring more, mainly for AI implementation and IT support. Nine had cut contracted work such as software development, customer service, legal counsel and back-office jobs, much of it already offshore. Of 100 pieces of software interviewees described building with AI, 80% automated work that had been manual and 20% replaced software bought from vendors. The biggest gains came where companies reorganised work, for example giving people ownership of whole workflows and moving staff to the tasks AI cannot do, such as review and sales.
stories.matters: The first effect on jobs here is fewer openings, not firings. That falls first on graduates, contractors and outsourcing firms rather than on current staff.
stories.imply: These are Anthropic’s own customers, not a random sample, and Anthropic sells the tools. Read it as interviews that show patterns, not a count of jobs.
uses: If you manage a team, list which tasks AI now speeds up and which bottlenecks, like review or sales, now need more people.
Before automating a workflow from the top down, involve the experts who do it; the study found their resistance can stall these projects.
If you rely on outsourced back-office work, ask your provider how they use AI and what that means for price and quality.
stories.example: An operations head at a law firm moves a paralegal from filing to checking AI-drafted documents, rather than hiring a second person for the growing caseload.
stories.audience: Managers, HR and workforce planners, early-career workers and buyers of outsourced services.
stories.watch: Whether official hiring data starts to show the same pattern, and whether other AI labs publish similar studies of their customers.

source.title: Anthropic (Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory): Working with AI, 23 November 2026
source.quote: People at two-thirds of the companies we spoke to reported reduced hiring due to AI: as one person put it, “We may not be firing, but we’re not hiring.”

stories.theme: Virginia and Oregon became the first US states to sue SpaceX over sexual deepfakes made with Grok
stories.changed: On 22 and 23 November 2026 the attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia filed separate consumer-protection lawsuits against SpaceX, which owns X and xAI (now SpaceX Super Intelligence), over Grok’s image tools. They allege that Grok could turn a single real photo into nude or sexual images of people, including children, without consent, that a “spicy mode” was promoted, and that the company misled users by saying strong safeguards were in place. Virginia cites a Center for Countering Digital Hate estimate that Grok created and posted about 3 million sexualised images on X between 29 December 2025 and 8 January 2026, about 23,000 of which appeared to show children. Both states want court orders for stronger safeguards, civil penalties, the return of profits and legal costs; Virginia also seeks restitution for consumers. SpaceX told CNBC it acts against accounts that try to break its safeguards and notifies law enforcement. CNBC says these are the first state lawsuits; SpaceX also faces private suits and probes in the UK, Spain, Ireland, France and California.
stories.matters: States are using ordinary consumer-protection law, not new AI laws, to hold an AI maker to its safety claims. Any company that markets an AI tool as safe could face the same test.
stories.imply: What a vendor says about its safeguards can become evidence. Firms that let staff or customers generate images should check that filters, reporting and takedowns actually work.
uses: If your product generates images, test whether it can be made to alter a real person’s photo, and keep a log of what you block.
Check public safety claims on your website and in sales decks against what the product really does.
Set up a fast process for taking down abusive images and reporting them to the authorities.
stories.example: A marketing agency that uses an AI image tool bans uploads of real people’s photos without written consent and keeps each consent form on file.
stories.audience: Trust and safety teams, legal and marketing teams, and anyone deploying image-generation tools.
stories.watch: Whether the courts accept the cases, whether other states join, and whether SpaceX relies on Section 230, the US law that shields platforms from liability for users’ posts.

source.title: Virginia Office of the Attorney General: Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield file suit against SpaceX, 23 November 2026
source.quote: With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent.

stories.theme: Z.ai’s GLM-5.4 runs its own layers twice to think deeper; you can try it in the GLM Coding Plan, but the weights are not out yet
stories.changed: On 23 November 2026 Z.ai (Zhipu) released GLM-5.4, its first flagship built as a ‘loop transformer’: at the 750B scale it runs 28 layers of its GLM-5 base twice, adding depth without adding parameters. It adds vision, accepting text, image, video and file inputs with a 1M-token context and up to 128K tokens of output, and aims at what Z.ai calls generalised coding, such as CAD, 3D modelling and games. It is available now in the GLM Coding Plan, ZCode and Z.ai Chat, with weekly quotas 1.5 times those of GLM-5.3. API access and open weights are promised after safety checks, with no date or licence given. VentureBeat says Z.ai published no coding benchmarks for GLM-5.4 itself; its controlled evidence comes from a 30B test model. One early tester said it took 431 minutes to finish his coding tests against 109 for Gemini 4 Neon, but recommended it for code review and hunting security bugs.
stories.matters: Chinese labs keep finding ways to get more out of a model without making it bigger. If the weights arrive, teams could run a strong coding model on their own servers.
stories.imply: For now it is a subscription product without published benchmarks. Speed is a known weak spot, and Z.ai says it can get caught in overly long reasoning.
uses: If you already pay for the GLM Coding Plan, try it as a second reviewer on a pull request.
Give it slow, careful jobs like security review rather than quick edits.
Wait for the open weights and their licence before planning to run it yourself.
stories.example: A small security team runs GLM-5.4 overnight over one service’s code to list possible vulnerabilities, and an engineer checks each finding in the morning.
stories.audience: Developers on Z.ai plans, teams weighing open models, and security reviewers.
stories.watch: API pricing, the open-weight release and its licence, and independent benchmark results.

source.title: VentureBeat: Z.ai’s GLM-5.4 aims to match models up to four times its size by running 28 layers twice, 23 November 2026
source.quote: GLM-5.4 loops 28 layers of the GLM-5 base for two iterations at the 750B scale, adapted from an already pre-trained model through continued training.
